To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“Interferon induction in vivo increases the number and lytic activity of natural killer (NK) cells in the murine peripheral blood and lungs.”
“The NK‐lytic activity and the total number of NK cells are highly increased in the peripheral blood and lungs after interferon induction in vivo.”
(i) NK cells are increased in number in peripheral blood and lungs after interferon induction in vivo and (ii) NK cells have increased lytic activity after interferon induction.

the NK cells, in contrast to T cells, are not a homogeneous cell population, and that they have the ability to increase their numbers in vivo after stimulation by interferon, and that they are able to migrate to the lungs and other organs.
NK cells are not only activated by interferon, but also increased in number.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NK cell system is highly inducible by interferon in vivo and that the NK activity and number of NK cells can be increased in the peripheral blood, in the spleen and especially in the lungs.
the NK‐activity is highly increased in all lymphoid compartments and also in the lungs after the induction of interferon in the body.

the NK‐activity in the body is highly inducible by interferon, and that the increase in the number and activity of NK cells can be seen not only in the spleen, but also in the peripheral blood and lungs.
The main takeaway from our work is that

NK cell activity can be induced in vivo by interferon, and that this induction can be measured as increased lytic activity of NK cells, and as an increase in the number and percentage of LGLs and TBC in different lymphoid organs.
the number of NK cells in the lungs is increased by interferon, and this could be of importance in the defense of the lung against viral and tumor cells.
